messages.subject: Random sample and CFA/SEM
parts:
Dear List,

I have a very simple question that can reflect my (mis)understanding of CFA/SEM. Here some background:

 In the context of a proposal for developing an instrument, I describe the field test to evaluate the psychometrics properties of it (construct validity using CFA and maybe also SEM) by saying I will be using a random sample of the population of interest (middle school students). A colleague  of mine asked me whether the random sample would have any impact of the results of the CFA or SEM.

I could not answer him, but I have the idea that the parameter estimates (and estimation theory more broadly) makes sense when the data underlying the model come from a random sample, is that correct? Or it is the same to use a random or a convenience sample on which to apply CFA/SEM?


Thank you!

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Random sample and CFA/SEM
parts:
Yes, CFA / SEM statistical theory for making inferences to a population assumes a random sample from that population.  CFA / SEM does not differ from other methods in this regard.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: RE: Random sample and CFA/SEM
parts:
From examples in the applied literature, you would not know that sampling plan mattered, as with so many other aspects of inference.  If you had asked, “Will it make a difference to reviewers and editors?”, I might have replied, “It depends on your journal, but probably it does not matter.”  It *is* possible that the additional apparent complexity of these methods encourages readers to forget about basic issues like sampling.

     Cars are the same way, eh?  Once the engine gets complicated enough, it no longer needs petrol <g>.

--Ed Rigdon
